title: Attributes of a Good Independent Director
keywords: thirst for knowledge courage searching questions integrity hard work

primary_topics: Forum address on 'The Attributes and Challenges of a Great Independent Director,' October 19, 2015 -- invited by President Gil L. Gonzales on the general theme of 'Board Independence: Reality or Myth?'
CJP's five attributes of a Good Independent Director (GID): (1) thirst for knowledge, (2) courage, (3) ability to ask searching questions, (4) integrity, (5) passion for hard work and communication
CJP's objection to SEC administrative fiat restricting term limits, number of seats, and age qualifications of IDs -- only Congress has the power to legislate on voting rights
The ID's prime duty: fiduciary fidelity to the corporation above and beyond private interests -- differentiated from executive and non-executive directors by the very independence they carry
sub_topics: Why CJP prefers 'Good' over 'Great' ID: the word 'great' implies 'fantastic or extraordinary expertise'; the left-eye specialist joke -- 'an expert is one who knows more and more about less and less. So the ultimate expert is one who knows everything about nothing!'

ID basics: must own at least one share of stock; elected per Corporation Code; all directors are trustees or fiduciaries; prime duty is to promote and uphold the welfare of the corporation above and beyond individual/private interests

Definition of independence: SEC Securities Regulation Code -- 'a person other than an officer or employee of the corporation, its parent or subsidiaries, or any other individual having a relationship with the corporation, which would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment'

Objection to administrative term/seat/age limits: Corporation Code grants shareholders the right to vote and be voted without such limitations; 'just like the right to suffrage in a democracy, is a basic right in a corporate polity that cannot be restricted or limited by mere administrative regulation. Only Congress has the power to legislate on them'
Attribute 1 -- Thirst for knowledge: basic knowledge of Corporation Code, SRC, and SEC issuances; financial statements and GAAP/audit principles; the specific corporation they serve
Attribute 2 -- Courage: uphold zealously laws, articles and bylaws, canons of corporate ethics, manual of corporate governance; 'advocates of transparency and timely disclosures'

Attribute 3 -- Ability to ask searching questions: business of PLCs is often complicated; 'many times, even the most assiduous IDs cannot have enough knowledge to guide them in making intelligent decisions without asking searching questions'

Attribute 4 -- Integrity: 'not mere honesty; it includes intellectual decency and a deep sense of personal honor. Persons of true integrity judge themselves not only by their outward acts but by their intentions which are known only to them and to God. To have integrity implies moral courage.'
Attribute 5 -- Passion for hard work and communication: organizing thoughts and communicating them well, verbally and in writing
Three summary challenges: (1) fidelity to corporation above private interest; (2) live up to independence mandate (free of prohibited relationships); (3) embody the five attributes

stances.claim: The SEC's proposed administrative regulations limiting ID term limits, number of board seats, and age qualifications are illegal and unreasonable -- they restrict shareholders' fundamental right to vote and be voted, a right equivalent to suffrage in a democracy that only Congress, not the SEC, can limit. CJP 'consistently resisted' these attempts.
stances.rhetorical_move: suffrage-equivalence argument: the right to vote and be voted as a constitutional-grade right that administrative fiat cannot override
stances.confidence: asserted as a firm legal position with explicit consistency over time

stances.claim: Integrity is the most profound of the five GID attributes because it encompasses not just honesty but 'intellectual decency and a deep sense of personal honor' -- persons of true integrity judge themselves by their intentions, known only to them and to God. It implies moral courage, making it the master virtue that enables the other four.
stances.rhetorical_move: integrity-as-master-virtue: the internal-accountability standard (intentions known only to God) as the deepest and most demanding dimension of the five
stances.confidence: asserted as the culminating attribute in the enumeration

stances.claim: Downgrading the target from 'Great' to 'Good' Independent Director is not false modesty but epistemological precision -- 'great' implies the expert who knows everything about nothing, whereas 'good' is a 'more modest and achievable ambition' that actually describes what the role requires.
stances.rhetorical_move: epistemological-precision argument: the expert-joke as a philosophical refusal of the 'great' label in favor of a more honest standard
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing conceptual choice for the entire speech

notable_anecdotes: The left-eye specialist joke: a high school friend who specialized in eye diseases told CJP 'Art, I am sorry I cannot help you' about his right eye problem -- 'I am a great expert only of the left eye.' CJP's point: 'an expert is one who knows more and more about less and less. So the ultimate expert is one who knows everything about nothing!'

CJP's objection to SEC administrative fiat: 'I have consistently resisted attempts to limit, through administrative fiat, the terms of office of directors, or their number of seats, or their age qualifications' -- framing the resistance as a matter of constitutional principle (only Congress can legislate on voting rights), not personal interest.

Integrity defined beyond honesty: 'Persons of true integrity judge themselves not only by their outward acts but by their intentions which are known only to them and to God.' -- the internal conscience as the ultimate accountability mechanism.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 19, 2015 at a forum on 'Board Independence: Reality or Myth?' -- organized in the context of the SEC's Corporate Governance Blueprint Project -- this address by CJP immediately reframes the invitation topic: he was asked to speak on 'great' independent directors but prefers 'good,' illustrated by the left-eye specialist joke ('an expert is one who knows more and more about less and less; the ultimate expert knows everything about nothing'). He outlines the fundamentals: IDs must own at least one share, are elected per the Corporation Code, are trustees with prime fiduciary duty to the corporation above their own interests, and are defined by the Securities Regulation Code as free of relationships that would interfere with independent judgment. He objects -- as he has 'consistently' -- to SEC administrative fiat limiting ID term limits, number of seats, and age qualifications: 'The right to vote and be voted directors, just like the right to suffrage in a democracy, is a basic right in a corporate polity that cannot be restricted or limited by mere administrative regulation. Only Congress has the power to legislate on them.' He then enumerates five attributes of a Good ID: (1) thirst for knowledge (Corporation Code, SRC, SEC issuances, financial statements, the specific corporation); (2) courage (zealous upholding of laws, articles, bylaws, ethics, governance manuals; advocates of transparency and disclosure); (3) ability to ask searching questions (PLCs are complicated; intelligence requires questions, not just information); (4) integrity -- 'not mere honesty; it includes intellectual decency and a deep sense of personal honor. Persons of true integrity judge themselves not only by their outward acts but by their intentions which are known only to them and to God. To have integrity implies moral courage'; and (5) passion for hard work and communication (verbal and written). He summarizes three challenges: fidelity to the corporation, living up to independence, and embodying the five attributes.
